title: Biryani by Any Other Name: Haridwar's Push to Rename India's Favourite Dish Stirs a Global Food Fight
excerpt: Hindu priests in the holy city are forcing vendors to relabel vegetarian biryani as pulao — but India's 93 million annual biryani orders suggest the dish will outlast the campaign.
body:
In the holy Hindu city of Haridwar, where the Ganges tumbles out of the Himalayan foothills and the air is thick with the aroma of cinnamon, cumin, and nutmeg, a new battle has erupted — not over territory or politics, but over a word on a menu.

Members of the Akhand Parshuram Akhada, a Hindu priests' organisation, have launched a campaign ordering street food vendors to stop using the word "biryani" on their signboards. In its place, they want "veg pulao." Their reasoning: biryani is etymologically and culturally linked to meat-based preparations, and the word is therefore inappropriate in one of Hinduism's holiest pilgrimage cities.

"Since the word biryani is associated with meat dishes, it is inappropriate for this holy land," Adhir Kaushik, a leader of the priests' group, told reporters this week. "We urge all vendors to co-operate to avoid any future conflict."

## A 500-Year-Old Dish Meets 21st-Century Identity Politics

The irony cuts deep. Haridwar already enforces a strict no-meat, no-egg zone within a 5-kilometre radius of the sacred Har-ki-Pauri ghat. The only "biryani" sold in the area is already vegetarian. What the priests are demanding is not a change in what's being cooked, but a change in what it's called.

Biryani's name derives from the Persian *birinj* (rice), a legacy of the Mughal conquerors who brought the dish to the Indian subcontinent in the 16th century. Under Mughal rule, it evolved into the richly layered, slow-cooked masterpiece served at banquets and weddings. The renaming campaign is part of a broader push by Hindu nationalist groups to erase vestiges of centuries-long Mughal influence across India — from street names and monuments to, now, restaurant menus.

But there's a culinary inconvenience the priests may have overlooked: "pulao" itself derives from *pilaf*, an ancient Persian term. The earliest written recipe for pulao dates to the 10th-century Persian scholar Avicenna.

## Chefs and Food Writers Push Back

India's food community has responded with a mix of bemusement and exasperation. "How can a biryani be vegetarian?" asked Shakeel Buchh, manager of Zahra's café in Delhi. "It has to have richly spiced chicken or mutton in it. If it doesn't, then it's pulao, which is a different dish and not half as delicious."

Food writer and TV host Rupa Balachandar pointed to the technical differences: biryani requires yakhni (meat stock) and a layering technique where partially boiled rice is stacked over separately cooked meat. Pulao, by contrast, cooks rice and vegetables together in one pot.

"By definition, biryani is made with yakhni, and if you don't have the stock it's not biryani but pulao," Balachandar said. Food writer Karen Anand noted that vendors deliberately use the biryani label because it signals something more upmarket. "When you call it biryani, it suggests it's more flavoursome. Vegetarian pulao probably comes across as ordinary."

## The Diaspora Angle: NRIs and the Biryani Bond

For the Indian diaspora, biryani is far more than a dish — it's a cultural anchor. In cities from Houston to London, biryani is the go-to comfort food at family gatherings, the centrepiece of Eid and Diwali parties alike, and the single most ordered item on Indian food delivery apps worldwide.

Last year alone, Swiggy — India's largest food delivery service — processed 93 million biryani orders, or roughly 194 plates every minute, making it the most ordered dish for the tenth consecutive year. Vegetarian biryani accounted for 35 million of those orders.

For NRIs watching from abroad, the Haridwar controversy touches a nerve. Biryani has become a symbol of India's syncretic food culture — a Mughal inheritance that Hindus, Muslims, Christians, and Sikhs have all claimed, adapted, and loved. Attempts to erase its name feel, to many, like an erasure of that shared heritage.

## What's Next

Whether Haridwar's vendors will comply remains to be seen. Shahid Ahmed, a biryani seller in south Delhi, captured the futility of the exercise: "One is royal. The other is homely. I'd never try to sell pulao because it's so easy to make at home."

India has renamed cities, forts, and railway stations in recent years. But 93 million orders suggest biryani might just be un-renameable.
